This modest birth mass is characteristic of a species that relies on an extended period of intense maternal investment within the confines of a winter den. The cubs, typically born as altricial neonates, are entirely dependent on their mother's lipid-rich milk during the initial weeks of life. Lactation onset occurs almost immediately following the birth event, and the cubs transition through a suckling juvenile stage that is critical for their survival. The period of maternal dependency is substantial, with weaning occurring at 876 days after birth [tx = 876 days after birth] for cubs under typical Arctic conditions and at a standard body temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C]. This prolonged dependency allows the cubs to gain sufficient body mass and develop the hunting skills necessary to survive on the sea ice habitat before they achieve full nutritional independence.

Reproduction in polar bears is tightly linked to the seasonal availability of their primary prey, ringed seals. This period is almost entirely confined to the time during which the female is resident in her maternity den. This slow reproductive rate is an adaptation to the low primary productivity of the Arctic marine ecosystem, where high maternal investment is essential for cub survival through their first winter.

This remarkable growth is fueled by the extraordinarily high fat content of polar bear milk, which can exceed thirty percent lipid during peak lactation. This sexual dimorphism in maturation reflects the intense intrasexual competition among males for access to breeding females.

Adult male polar bears are among the largest terrestrial carnivores, with a maximum recorded head-body length of 225 centimeters [Li = 225 centimeters] and an ultimate wet weight for males reaching an impressive 389,000 grams [Wwi = 389,000 grams]. Females are considerably smaller, attaining a maximum head-body length of 194 centimeters [Li = 194 centimeters] and a mature body mass of 185 kilograms [Wwi = 185 kilograms] when in prime condition. This pronounced sexual dimorphism is driven by the polygynous mating system, where larger males have a competitive advantage in securing access to estrous females. The species exhibits a k-selected life-history strategy characterized by slow growth, delayed reproduction, and high investment in relatively few offspring. Populations are currently threatened by climate-driven sea ice loss, which reduces access to their seal prey and disrupts denning habitat.
